name: SAP LeanIX
tagline: SaaS for cataloging your application portfolio, its tech stack, and how it all maps to business capabilities.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. LeanIX is quote-based enterprise pricing, no public list price.

verdictSummary: The data model here is not hard: fact sheets with types, relations, lifecycle dates, and a few matrix reports. An agent will give you that in a sitting, and for a solo architect or a ten-app startup it is genuinely enough. What you cannot one-shot is the thing LeanIX actually sells: pulling truth out of ServiceNow, cloud accounts, and SSO logs, then nagging four hundred application owners via surveys until the inventory stops being fiction. Add the reference catalog of vendor lifecycle and end-of-life dates, which is curated data you do not have. Build the local version if you want a personal portfolio map, but understand you are building the schema, not the product.
coreLoopDIY: A local app where you create typed fact sheets for applications, IT components, and business capabilities, link them, set lifecycle dates, and render portfolio matrix and roadmap views.
requirements: Your own portfolio data, entered or imported by hand as CSV
whatYouLose: Automated discovery: ServiceNow CMDB, cloud account scans, SaaS management feeds that keep the inventory honest without manual entry
Surveys and workflows that collect data from hundreds of application owners who do not care about your inventory
The curated vendor lifecycle and end-of-life reference catalog behind obsolescence risk reporting
SSO, SCIM, audit trails, role-based access, and the reporting formats auditors and CIOs expect
A shared source of truth: a local app on your laptop is a diagram, not a governance system
moatNotes: Once the whole portfolio graph, its survey history, and the exec reports live in one tool, moving is a multi-quarter project nobody volunteers for.
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody buys an EAM tool because the schema is clever. They buy it because somebody above them wants one defensible answer to "what software do we run, who owns it, what breaks if we retire it, and what goes end-of-life next year", and that answer has to come from systems of record rather than a spreadsheet maintained by one person who is leaving. The integrations, the survey machinery, the lifecycle catalog, and the ability to hand a board-ready report to a CIO are the product. A self-built version serves exactly one honest use case: a small portfolio where you are the only data source anyway.
notes: You can clone the fact sheet model in a weekend and it will even look decent. The moat is the integration plumbing that keeps the inventory true plus a curated vendor lifecycle catalog, neither of which you can type in by hand.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user enterprise architecture catalog. Call it Portfolio.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, SQLite via better-sqlite3 with Drizzle ORM, Tailwind for styling. Everything runs locally with `npm run dev`. No auth, no accounts, no cloud services, no telemetry. If any secret is ever needed, read it from .env and ship .env.example.

Data model: a single `factsheets` table with fields id, type, name, description, owner, lifecyclePhase, lifecycleDates (JSON: plan, phaseIn, active, phaseOut, endOfLife), tags, customFields (JSON). Allowed types: application, itComponent, businessCapability, interface, provider. A separate `relations` table with fromId, toId, relationType, description. Relations are directional but always rendered both ways.

Screens:
1. Inventory: filterable, sortable table of fact sheets with type and lifecycle phase filters, plus full-text search over name and description.
2. Fact sheet detail: edit all fields inline, manage relations with a type-aware picker, show a lifecycle timeline bar.
3. Portfolio matrix: pick two axes from any numeric or enum custom field (for example businessCriticality and technicalFit) and plot applications as a bubble grid, bubble size from a third field.
4. Capability map: business capabilities as cards, each listing the applications linked to it, colored by worst lifecycle phase among them.
5. Roadmap: Gantt-style horizontal bars from lifecycleDates, grouped by type, with a year scale.

Also build: CSV import and export for both tables, with a dry-run preview that reports rows it cannot match. Seed the database with about 25 realistic fact sheets and 40 relations so every screen has something to show on first run.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build or stub: SSO, multi-user permissions, surveys, approval workflows, ServiceNow or cloud discovery connectors, any vendor end-of-life data source. Leave a short README section called "What this is not" that says the inventory is only as true as what you type into it.

Keep it to one process and one SQLite file. Write a README with setup, the data model, and how to reset the database.
